subject: Surgery
title: Fluid and Electrolyte Balance in Surgical Patients

source.title: Fluid and Electrolyte Balance in Surgical Patients

objectives: Classify hyponatraemia into dilutional and depletional types and treat each correctly.
Recognise sodium excess and explain why serum sodium is an unreliable guide.
Explain the causes, ECG changes and safe treatment of hypokalaemia.
Manage hyperkalaemia in the correct sequence of protect, shift and remove.
State daily fluid and electrolyte requirements and the routes of replacement.
Compare crystalloids and colloids and recall standard crystalloid compositions.
Prescribe a standard maintenance regimen and adjust for losses and pyrexia.

sections.title: Hyponatraemia
sections.digest: Normal serum sodium is **135–145 mmol/L**; **hyponatraemia** is <135 mmol/L. In surgery it is either **dilutional (hypervolaemic)** or **depletional (hypovolaemic)**. Dilutional causes: excess salt-free fluid (5% dextrose), post-operative **ADH** excess, cirrhosis and heart failure. Depletional causes: gastrointestinal losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, obstruction, fistulae — GI secretions have near-plasma sodium), ECF loss in burns or third-space sequestration (peritonitis, ileus, ascites), and renal loss (salt-losing nephritis, diuretics, adrenal failure). Most patients with Na⁺ >120 mmol/L are asymptomatic; below that, cerebral symptoms (agitation, disorientation, delirium, vomiting, headache, seizures) reflect water shift into brain cells. Depletional signs are those of a low ECF: sunken eyes, dry coated tongue, collapsed peripheral veins, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, low CVP and scanty dark urine. **Treatment:** dilutional → restrict water, and give **hypertonic (3%) saline** only if severe (<120 mmol/L) or with neurological signs; depletional → restore ECF with **normal saline (0.9%)** or Hartmann's. Correct slowly — rapid correction risks **central pontine myelinolysis**.
highYield: Hyponatraemia = serum Na⁺ <135 mmol/L.
Symptoms are mostly cerebral once Na⁺ <120 mmol/L.
Severe/symptomatic dilutional hyponatraemia → hypertonic (3%) saline.
Correct slowly — rapid correction causes central pontine myelinolysis.
Serum sodium does NOT measure total body sodium.
pitfalls: Do not correct hyponatraemia rapidly → central pontine myelinolysis.
A normal serum sodium can hide a large total-body sodium deficit.

sections.title: Hypernatraemia
sections.digest: **Sodium excess (hypernatraemia)** in surgery follows excessive 0.9% saline in the early post-operative period, when sodium retention is expected, overloading the circulation with salt and water. Other causes: **hyperaldosteronism** — primary (**Conn's syndrome**) or secondary (cirrhosis) — and **Cushing's syndrome** (hyperadrenocorticism). Clinically the only reliable sign of total-body sodium excess is **oedema**; early there is slight facial puffiness, then weight gain paralleling ECF accumulation, and hypertension. Serum sodium is often normal. **Treatment:** sodium restriction and careful diuretics.
highYield: The only reliable sign of total-body sodium excess is oedema.
Post-op excess 0.9% saline is the classic surgical cause.
Serum sodium is usually normal despite sodium excess.
pitfalls: Serum sodium is a poor guide to total body sodium; judge by oedema and weight.

sections.title: Hypokalaemia
sections.digest: Serum potassium is a small fraction of total body potassium, so small serum falls reflect large losses. **Causes of hypokalaemia:** excessive vomiting (pyloric stenosis, obstruction, ileus) and prolonged gastroduodenal aspiration replaced with saline; alimentary fistulae; severe diarrhoea (cholera, ulcerative colitis, villous tumour, ileostomy); loop diuretics (furosemide); **alkalosis** (shift into cells without true loss); and hyperaldosteronism. **Consequences:** it raises membrane excitation potentials, making nerves/muscles *less* excitable; risk of supraventricular arrhythmias; and predisposition to hepatic coma in liver disease. **Clinical:** often asymptomatic; early malaise/weakness with slow slurred speech; paralytic ileus and distension; and, with severe depletion, respiratory-muscle weakness. **ECG:** prolonged QT, ST depression, T-wave flattening/inversion and a **U wave**. **Treatment:** deficit ≈ (4.5 − serum K) × 100; add potassium to the infusion spread over the day — never a bolus. Safe rules: urine output ≥40 mL/h, ≤40 mmol per litre, and no faster than 40 mmol/h.
highYield: Small serum K fall = large total-body deficit.
ECG of hypokalaemia: flat/inverted T, ST depression, prolonged QT, U wave.
Never give potassium as a bolus — it causes fatal arrhythmia.
Safe potassium: urine ≥40 mL/h, ≤40 mmol/L, ≤40 mmol/h.

tables.title: Safe rules for giving IV potassium

pitfalls: Potassium is dangerous: hyperkalaemia from over-rapid replacement causes arrhythmia and asystole.
Alkalosis lowers serum K by an intracellular shift, not by true depletion.

sections.title: Hyperkalaemia
sections.digest: Life-threatening **hyperkalaemia** usually needs **renal failure**, worsened by tissue destruction or by sodium/calcium depletion; **acidosis** shifts potassium out of cells (diabetics with low insulin are prone). **Consequences:** a rise to ~5 mmol/L stimulates aldosterone (renal K excretion); it lowers membrane excitation potentials, making cells more excitable, and above ~7 mmol/L intracardiac conduction slows with arrhythmia, bradycardia, hypotension and cardiac arrest. **ECG** (a sensitive test) shows a **wide QRS and peaked T waves**. **Treatment (in order):** IV **calcium gluconate** (antagonises potassium at the membrane), IV **sodium bicarbonate** (alkalinisation shifts K into cells), **dextrose + insulin** (10 units insulin with 20 g glucose drives K in with glycogen; dextrose prevents hypoglycaemia), then **ion-exchange resin** (sodium polystyrene sulfonate, orally or by enema) and, if all fail, **dialysis**.
highYield: Hyperkalaemia usually needs renal failure to be dangerous.
ECG: peaked T waves then a wide QRS.
Calcium gluconate protects the myocardium but does not lower K.
Insulin+dextrose and bicarbonate shift K into cells; resin/dialysis remove it.

tables.title: Potassium ECG changes
rows: Flat/inverted T, ST depression, long QT, U wave

pitfalls: Calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium but does not remove potassium — always follow it with shifting/removing measures.

sections.title: Requirements & routes
sections.digest: Daily adult requirements: **water ~35 mL/kg**, **sodium ~1 mmol/kg**, **potassium ~1 mmol/kg**. Routes: **enteral (oral)** when the GI tract works and the deficit is modest (not possible in post-operative ileus); **parenteral (IV)** when the gut is not working or rapid replacement is needed. Parenteral fluids divide into **crystalloid**, **colloid** and **blood**. Prescribing considers three things: **basal requirements**, **continuing abnormal losses**, and **pre-existing dehydration/electrolyte loss**. Add ~200 mL/day per 1°C of pyrexia, and add insensible/other losses to the total.
highYield: Daily adult: water 35 mL/kg, Na 1 mmol/kg, K 1 mmol/kg.
Prescribe for basal needs + ongoing losses + pre-existing deficit.
Add ~200 mL/day for each 1°C rise in temperature.
pitfalls: Oral replacement fails in paralytic ileus — use the IV route.

sections.title: Types of fluid
sections.digest: **Water** is given as 5% dextrose (dextrose is metabolised, leaving free water). **Crystalloids** are isotonic salt solutions. **Colloids** hold larger molecules in the intravascular space: **albumin 4.5%** (natural, no clotting factors, small anaphylaxis risk, expensive); **gelatins** (Haemaccel/Gelofusine, from bovine collagen, half-life 8–10 h — Haemaccel contains K⁺ and Ca²⁺ so it clots citrated blood in a shared giving set); **dextrans** (glucose polymers, Dextran 40 filtered by kidney, Dextran 70 stays longer; interfere with cross-matching and coagulation via rouleaux, nephrotoxic, allergenic); and **hetastarch** (6% in saline, half-life 16–24 h, limit dose, no cross-match interference, expensive).
highYield: 5% dextrose = a way of giving free water.
Haemaccel contains K⁺/Ca²⁺ → clots citrated blood in a shared line.
Dextrans interfere with cross-matching and coagulation (rouleaux).

tables.title: Colloids
rows: Bovine collagen; Haemaccel has K⁺/Ca²⁺ → clots citrated blood
Long half-life; no cross-match interference; expensive

pitfalls: Never run Haemaccel through the same giving set as citrated blood — residual blood clots.
Dextran can invalidate a subsequent cross-match — take the sample first.

sections.title: Crystalloid compositions
sections.digest: Know the crystalloid contents. **Physiological (normal) saline 0.9%**: Na⁺ 154, Cl⁻ 154 mmol/L. **Dextrose 5%**: 278 mmol/L dextrose (negligible calories, effectively free water). **Dextrose-saline** (0.18% saline, 4% dextrose): Na⁺ 30, Cl⁻ 30 mmol/L. **Hartmann's solution**: Na⁺ 131, K⁺ 5, Cl⁻ 111, HCO₃⁻ 29, Ca²⁺ 2 mmol/L. **Ringer's solution**: Na⁺ 147, K⁺ 4, Cl⁻ 156, Ca²⁺ 2.2 mmol/L. Hartmann's/Ringer's are the balanced options closest to plasma.
highYield: Normal saline = Na⁺ 154, Cl⁻ 154.
Hartmann's contains Na, K, Cl, bicarbonate and calcium (near-plasma).
Dextrose-saline delivers little sodium (Na⁺ 30).
pitfalls: Avoid potassium-containing Hartmann's as the sole fluid in established hyperkalaemia/renal failure.

sections.title: Basal fluid regimens
sections.digest: Standard daily maintenance for a 70-kg adult. **Regimen A:** 1 L normal saline + 20 mmol KCl over 8 h, then 1 L 5% dextrose + 20 mmol KCl over 8 h, then another 1 L 5% dextrose + 20 mmol KCl over 8 h — giving 3 L water, 60 mmol K⁺, 150 mmol Na⁺. **Regimen B:** 3 × (1 L dextrose-saline + 20 mmol KCl over 8 h) — giving 3 L water, 60 mmol K⁺, 90 mmol Na⁺; since metabolised dextrose effectively delivers hypotonic saline, regimen B suits only the short term. Add 200 mL/day per 1°C pyrexia and all measured/insensible losses.
highYield: Regimen A ≈ 3 L water, 150 mmol Na, 60 mmol K.
Regimen B (dextrose-saline) suits only the short term.
Add for fever and losses on top of maintenance.

tables.title: Maintenance regimens (70-kg adult / 24 h)
rows: 1 L saline + 2 L 5% dextrose, each +20 mmol KCl/8 h
3 L dextrose-saline, each +20 mmol KCl/8 h

pitfalls: Prolonged regimen B effectively gives hypotonic saline → dilutional hyponatraemia.

mnemonics.expansion: Hyperkalaemia treatment order: Calcium gluconate, Bicarbonate, Insulin+Glucose, K-binding resin, Dialysis
Hyperkalaemia effects: Muscle weakness, Urine (oliguria), Respiratory failure, Decreased contractility, ECG changes, Reflexes reduced

mnemonics.cue: From low to high the pons will die; from high to low the brain will blow
mnemonics.expansion: Correct hyponatraemia SLOWLY (pontine myelinolysis) and hypernatraemia slowly (cerebral oedema)

cards.front: Define hyponatraemia.
cards.back: Serum sodium below 135 mmol/L (normal 135–145).

cards.front: Name the two surgical categories of hyponatraemia.
cards.back: Dilutional (hypervolaemic) and depletional (hypovolaemic).

cards.cloze: Dilutional hyponatraemia can follow post-operative excess of {{c1::ADH}}.

cards.front: Give three depletional causes of hyponatraemia.
cards.back: GI losses (vomiting/diarrhoea/fistulae), ECF/third-space loss (burns, peritonitis, ascites), renal loss (diuretics, salt-losing nephritis, adrenal failure).

cards.front: Why are hyponatraemia symptoms mostly cerebral?
cards.back: Water shifts into brain cells (cerebral oedema) — agitation, delirium, seizures.

cards.cloze: Most patients with serum Na⁺ above {{c1::120}} mmol/L are asymptomatic.

cards.front: When is 3% (hypertonic) saline indicated in hyponatraemia?
cards.back: Severe (Na⁺ <120 mmol/L) or when neurological symptoms are present.

cards.front: What is the danger of correcting hyponatraemia too fast?
cards.back: Central pontine myelinolysis.

cards.front: How is depletional hyponatraemia treated?
cards.back: Restore ECF volume with normal saline (0.9%) or Hartmann's.

cards.front: Complication of over-rapid Na correction (two words).
cards.back: pontine myelinolysis

cards.front: What is the only reliable sign of total-body sodium excess?
cards.back: Oedema.

cards.front: Give the classic surgical cause of sodium excess.
cards.back: Excessive 0.9% saline in the early post-operative period.

cards.cloze: Primary hyperaldosteronism ({{c1::Conn's syndrome}}) causes sodium retention.

cards.front: Treatment of total-body sodium excess?
cards.back: Sodium restriction and careful use of diuretics.

cards.front: Why do small serum K falls matter?
cards.back: Serum K is a small part of total body K, so a small fall reflects a large deficit.

cards.front: Name four causes of hypokalaemia.
cards.back: Vomiting/aspiration, fistulae, severe diarrhoea, loop diuretics (also alkalosis, hyperaldosteronism).

cards.cloze: Alkalosis lowers serum potassium by shifting it {{c1::into cells}} without true loss.

cards.front: List the ECG changes of hypokalaemia.
cards.back: Prolonged QT, ST depression, flat/inverted T wave, and a U wave.

cards.front: Estimate the potassium deficit.
State the three safe rules for IV potassium.
cards.back: Urine ≥40 mL/h; ≤40 mmol per litre; no faster than 40 mmol/h (never a bolus).

cards.cloze: Potassium should never be given as a {{c1::bolus}}.

cards.front: What condition usually underlies dangerous hyperkalaemia?
cards.back: Renal failure (worsened by tissue destruction or Na/Ca depletion).

cards.cloze: {{c1::Acidosis}} shifts potassium out of cells into the ECF.

cards.front: Earliest ECG change of hyperkalaemia?
cards.back: Peaked (tented) T waves; later a wide QRS.

cards.front: First drug in hyperkalaemia and why?
cards.back: IV calcium gluconate — it antagonises potassium at the membrane (protects the heart) but does not lower K.

cards.front: How do insulin-dextrose and bicarbonate help hyperkalaemia?
cards.back: They shift potassium into cells (dextrose prevents hypoglycaemia with insulin).

cards.front: Which measures actually remove potassium from the body?
cards.back: Ion-exchange resin (via the gut) and dialysis.

cards.front: Antagonises potassium at the membrane without lowering serum K
cards.back: Calcium gluconate

cards.front: State the daily adult water, sodium and potassium requirements.
cards.back: Water ~35 mL/kg, sodium ~1 mmol/kg, potassium ~1 mmol/kg.

cards.front: What three components make up a fluid prescription?
cards.back: Basal requirements, continuing abnormal losses, and pre-existing dehydration/electrolyte loss.

cards.cloze: Add about {{c1::200 mL}} per day for each 1°C rise in body temperature.

cards.front: When is the enteral route unsuitable for fluid replacement?
cards.back: When the GI tract is not working, e.g. post-operative paralytic ileus.

cards.front: Why is 5% dextrose effectively a way of giving water?
cards.back: Dextrose is metabolised, leaving net free water.

cards.front: Why must Haemaccel not share a giving set with citrated blood?
cards.back: It contains K⁺ and Ca²⁺, which clot the residual citrated blood.

cards.cloze: Dextrans interfere with blood cross-matching and coagulation by forming red-cell {{c1::rouleaux}}.

cards.front: Name the three broad categories of parenteral fluid.
cards.back: Crystalloid, colloid and blood.

cards.cloze: Normal saline 0.9% contains Na⁺ {{c1::154}} mmol/L and Cl⁻ 154 mmol/L.

cards.front: Which ions does Hartmann's solution contain?
cards.back: Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, bicarbonate and calcium — close to plasma.

cards.front: Why is dextrose-saline a poor sodium source?
cards.back: It contains only ~30 mmol/L sodium.

cards.front: Sodium concentration of normal saline (number, mmol/L).
What does maintenance regimen A provide over 24 h?
cards.back: ~3 L water, 150 mmol Na⁺ and 60 mmol K⁺.

cards.front: Why is dextrose-saline regimen B only for the short term?
cards.back: Metabolised dextrose effectively delivers hypotonic saline → dilutional hyponatraemia.

cards.cloze: A standard bag of maintenance fluid typically carries {{c1::20}} mmol KCl over 8 hours.

cards.front: Why do GI secretion losses cause hyponatraemia?
cards.back: Most GI secretions have a sodium content close to plasma, so their loss depletes sodium.

cards.front: Which arrhythmia risk accompanies hypokalaemia?
cards.back: Supraventricular arrhythmias.

cards.front: Which patients are especially prone to hyperkalaemia from acidosis?
cards.back: Diabetics with reduced or absent insulin secretion.

cards.cloze: Gelatin colloids are modified from the hydrolysis of {{c1::bovine collagen}}.

cards.front: What early facial sign may appear in sodium excess?
cards.back: Slight puffiness of the face.

cards.front: Besides basal needs and fever, what else must be added to the fluid total?
cards.back: Continuing abnormal losses and any pre-existing dehydration/electrolyte deficit (including insensible loss).

cards.front: State the normal serum sodium range.

cards.cloze: Third-space losses causing depletional hyponatraemia include peritonitis, ileus and {{c1::ascites}}.

cards.front: Name three cerebral features of dilutional hyponatraemia.
cards.back: Agitation, disorientation/delirium and seizures (also headache and vomiting).

cards.front: First step for asymptomatic dilutional hyponatraemia?
cards.back: Restrict water intake.

cards.cloze: In depletional hyponatraemia the tongue is {{c1::coated and dry}} and peripheral veins are collapsed.

cards.front: Give two endocrine causes of sodium excess.
cards.back: Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's/secondary) and Cushing's syndrome.

cards.front: What parallels ECF accumulation in sodium excess?
cards.back: Weight gain (with hypertension).

cards.front: Only reliable sign of total-body sodium excess (one word).
cards.back: oedema

cards.front: Which diuretic classically causes hypokalaemia?
cards.back: Furosemide (a loop diuretic).

cards.front: How does hypokalaemia change nerve/muscle excitability?
cards.back: It raises membrane excitation potentials, making them less excitable.

cards.front: Which patients risk hepatic coma with hypokalaemia?
cards.back: Those with liver disease.

cards.cloze: Hypokalaemia depresses the {{c1::ST}} segment and flattens or inverts the T wave.

cards.front: Early clinical features of potassium depletion?
cards.back: Vague malaise and weakness with slow, slurred speech.

cards.front: Over what period is replacement potassium distributed?
cards.back: Spread throughout the day in the infusion (never a bolus).

cards.front: How does hyperkalaemia change membrane excitation potentials?
cards.back: It lowers them, making cells more excitable.

cards.cloze: Ion-exchange resin (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) can be given by mouth or by {{c1::enema}}.

cards.front: What is done if all pharmacological measures fail to lower potassium?
cards.back: Dialysis.

cards.front: Classic peaked ECG wave in hyperkalaemia (one word).
cards.back: T

cards.front: Daily sodium and potassium requirements per kg?
cards.back: About 1 mmol/kg each per day.

cards.front: Half-life of gelatin colloids?
cards.back: About 8–10 hours.

cards.front: Two problems associated with dextrans.
cards.back: Nephrotoxicity and interference with cross-matching/coagulation (rouleaux); also allergy.

cards.cloze: Hetastarch is 6% starch in saline with a half-life of about {{c1::16–24}} hours.

cards.front: Dextrose concentration in 5% dextrose (mmol/L)?
cards.back: 278 mmol/L (calories negligible).

cards.cloze: Hartmann's solution contains about {{c1::29}} mmol/L bicarbonate and 2 mmol/L calcium.

cards.front: Which two divalent-relevant ions does Ringer's solution contain beyond Na/Cl?
cards.back: Potassium (~4 mmol/L) and calcium (~2.2 mmol/L).

cards.front: What does regimen B provide over 24 h?
cards.back: ~3 L water, 90 mmol Na⁺ and 60 mmol K⁺.

cards.cloze: Add {{c1::200}} mL per day to maintenance for each 1°C rise in temperature.

cards.front: Into which three groups are parenteral fluids divided?
cards.back: Crystalloid, colloid and blood.

cards.front: What happens to urine in depletional hyponatraemia?
cards.back: It becomes scanty, dark and of high specific gravity.

cards.front: Standard insulin-dextrose regimen for hyperkalaemia?
cards.back: About 10 units of regular insulin with 20 g of glucose.

cards.front: Name two GI causes of hypokalaemia besides vomiting.
cards.back: Severe diarrhoea (cholera, ulcerative colitis) and alimentary fistulae.

cards.front: Serum sodium level in most sodium-excess states?
cards.back: Usually normal.

cards.cloze: Hyponatraemia is defined as a serum sodium below {{c1::135}} mmol/L.

cards.front: Name a renal cause of depletional hyponatraemia.
cards.back: Salt-losing nephritis, diuretics or adrenal failure.

cards.front: Which respiratory problem follows severe hypokalaemia?
cards.back: Respiratory-muscle weakness → inadequate ventilation and atelectasis.

cards.front: Which ECG test is sensitive for hyperkalaemia and what does it show first?
cards.back: The ECG; it shows peaked T waves, then a wide QRS.

cards.front: Difference in renal handling between Dextran 40 and Dextran 70?
cards.back: Dextran 40 is filtered by the kidney; Dextran 70 is not, so it stays in the circulation longer.

cards.cloze: Sodium bicarbonate lowers potassium by encouraging an {{c1::intracellular}} shift.

cards.front: Chloride concentration of normal saline?
cards.back: 154 mmol/L.

cards.front: Why must insensible losses be included in the fluid total?
cards.back: They are ongoing water losses (skin/respiration) additional to measured output.

cards.front: Which post-operative physiological tendency contributes to sodium excess?
cards.back: Early post-operative sodium retention.

cards.front: Are most hypokalaemic patients symptomatic?
cards.back: No — most are asymptomatic.

cards.front: How is a fever accounted for in a fluid regimen?
cards.back: Add ~200 mL/day per 1°C rise, plus all measured and insensible losses.

mcqs.stem: A post-operative patient given large volumes of 5% dextrose becomes confused with serum Na⁺ 118 mmol/L. The most appropriate treatment is:

options.text: Rapid infusion of 3% saline to normalise Na⁺ within 2 hours
options.why: Rapid correction risks central pontine myelinolysis.

options.text: Water restriction and cautious hypertonic (3%) saline

options.why: Does not safely correct symptomatic hyponatraemia here.

explanation: This is dilutional hyponatraemia from salt-free fluid.
Because it is severe and symptomatic, cautious 3% saline plus water restriction is used.
Correction must be slow to avoid pontine myelinolysis.
keyFacts: Severe symptomatic dilutional hyponatraemia → cautious 3% saline, correct slowly.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Correct symptomatic hyponatraemia carefully, not quickly.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about serum sodium is correct?

options.why: Serum sodium does not reflect total body sodium.

options.text: It may be normal despite a large total-body sodium change
It is always low in sodium excess
options.why: Sodium excess often has a normal serum value.

options.text: It is unaffected by water balance

explanation: Serum sodium is a concentration, not a content.
It can be normal despite large total-body changes.

mcqs.stem: The only reliable clinical sign of total-body sodium excess is:

options.why: A feature but not the reliable sign.
Not the reliable sign of sodium excess.

explanation: Sodium excess expands the ECF.
The reliable sign is oedema; serum sodium is often normal.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Judge sodium excess by oedema, not the lab value.

mcqs.stem: A patient with pyloric stenosis and prolonged vomiting is most likely to develop:
explanation: GI losses and aspiration deplete potassium.
Pyloric stenosis is a classic cause of hypokalaemia (with alkalosis).

mcqs.stem: Which ECG feature is characteristic of hypokalaemia?
explanation: Hypokalaemia gives flat/inverted T, ST depression and prolonged QT.
A U wave is characteristic.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Match electrolyte to its ECG signature.

mcqs.stem: What is the single most important safety rule when replacing potassium intravenously?

options.text: Give it as a rapid bolus
Never give it as a bolus; infuse it

options.why: Concentration must be controlled, not maximised.

options.text: Withhold it if urine output is high
options.why: Adequate urine output is required, not a reason to withhold.

explanation: Bolus potassium causes arrhythmia and asystole.
Infuse it: urine ≥40 mL/h, ≤40 mmol/L, ≤40 mmol/h.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Potassium is lethal if given fast.

mcqs.stem: A dialysis patient has serum K⁺ 7.2 mmol/L with peaked T waves. The FIRST drug is:

options.why: Shifts K but is not the first membrane-protecting step.
Shifts K but not the first step for membrane protection.
An adjunct, not the first step here.

explanation: Calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium at once.
It buys time while shifting/removing measures work.
keyFacts: Calcium gluconate first in dangerous hyperkalaemia.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Protect the heart before lowering potassium.

mcqs.stem: Which measure actually REMOVES potassium from the body?
explanation: Calcium protects; insulin/bicarbonate/salbutamol shift.
Only resin and dialysis remove potassium from the body.
keyFacts: Resin/dialysis remove K; the rest shift or protect.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Distinguish protect vs shift vs remove.

mcqs.stem: Why should Haemaccel not be co-administered with citrated blood through the same giving set?

options.text: It contains K⁺ and Ca²⁺ that clot the residual blood

options.why: A dextran feature, not this one.

explanation: Haemaccel contains potassium and calcium.
Calcium reverses citrate anticoagulation, clotting residual blood in the set.
keyFacts: Haemaccel + citrated blood in one line → clot.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Beware calcium-containing colloids with citrated blood.

mcqs.stem: Which crystalloid most closely resembles plasma electrolytes?

options.why: Has only Na and Cl, no K/Ca/bicarbonate.
Correct — balanced with Na, K, Cl, bicarbonate, Ca.

explanation: Balanced crystalloids contain multiple physiological ions.
Hartmann's includes Na, K, Cl, bicarbonate and calcium.

mcqs.stem: Normal (physiological) saline 0.9% contains sodium at:

options.why: Too low; that is half-normal saline.
That is closer to Hartmann's sodium.
That is a dextrose figure, not sodium.

explanation: Normal saline is 0.9% NaCl.
This gives Na⁺ 154 and Cl⁻ 154 mmol/L.

mcqs.stem: The approximate daily water requirement for a healthy 70-kg adult is closest to:
explanation: Maintenance water is ~35 mL/kg/day.
For 70 kg this is roughly 2.5 L.

mcqs.stem: Prolonged use of dextrose-saline maintenance (regimen B) risks:

options.why: It provides little sodium, not excess.
Correct — metabolised dextrose effectively gives hypotonic saline.

explanation: After dextrose is metabolised, dextrose-saline behaves like hypotonic saline.
Prolonged use lowers sodium.

mcqs.stem: A patient with severe diarrhoea has sunken eyes, low CVP, tachycardia and Na⁺ 130 mmol/L. This is best treated with:

options.why: That treats dilutional, not depletional, hyponatraemia.
Not required at this level without severe symptoms.
Would worsen the sodium and not restore ECF.

explanation: The picture is hypovolaemic (depletional) hyponatraemia.
Restore ECF with normal saline or Hartmann's.

mcqs.stem: Insulin is given with dextrose in hyperkalaemia in order to:

options.why: Insulin shifts, it does not excrete K.

options.text: Drive potassium into cells while avoiding hypoglycaemia
Antagonise potassium at the myocardial membrane

explanation: Insulin drives potassium intracellularly with glycogen.
Dextrose is added to prevent hypoglycaemia.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Match each agent to its mechanism.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following causes hypokalaemia by an intracellular shift rather than true loss?
explanation: Most causes are true losses.
Alkalosis lowers serum K by an intracellular shift without depletion.

mcqs.stem: Which is a recognised cause of total-body sodium (and water) excess?

options.why: That causes sodium loss, not excess.

explanation: Aldosterone excess retains sodium and water.
Conn's syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism.

mcqs.stem: Which colloid is a natural blood product lacking clotting factors?

options.why: A modified bovine-collagen colloid, not a blood product.
A glucose polymer, not a blood product.

explanation: Albumin is a natural plasma protein.
The 4.5% preparation carries no clotting factors.
keyFacts: Albumin = natural colloid, no clotting factors.

mcqs.stem: A febrile surgical patient is 2°C above normal temperature. Roughly how much extra maintenance water should be added per day?
explanation: Add ~200 mL/day for each 1°C of pyrexia.
For 2°C that is about 400 mL.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Adjust maintenance for fever and losses.

mcqs.stem: Which acid–base disturbance predisposes to hyperkalaemia by shifting potassium out of cells?

options.why: Alkalosis shifts K in, lowering it.
The shift is driven by acidaemia.

explanation: Hydrogen ions exchange with potassium across the membrane.
Acidosis drives K out of cells, raising serum K.

mcqs.stem: Depletional hyponatraemia is characterised clinically by:

options.text: Low CVP, tachycardia and scanty dark urine
Marked thirst as the dominant feature
options.why: Thirst is less prominent in salt-and-water depletion.

explanation: Depletion reduces ECF volume.
Signs include low CVP, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension and scanty concentrated urine.

mcqs.stem: Maintenance regimen A over 24 hours provides approximately:

options.text: 3 L water, 90 mmol Na, 60 mmol K
3 L water, 150 mmol Na, 60 mmol K
2 L water, 150 mmol Na, 20 mmol K
3 L water, 300 mmol Na, 120 mmol K
1 L water, 60 mmol Na, 20 mmol K

explanation: Regimen A uses 1 L saline plus 2 L dextrose, each with 20 mmol KCl.
This gives ~3 L water, 150 mmol Na and 60 mmol K.

mcqs.stem: Which fluid effectively delivers pure water once metabolised?

options.why: Correct — dextrose is metabolised, leaving free water.

explanation: Dextrose is metabolised to CO2 and water.
5% dextrose therefore provides free water.

mcqs.stem: Dextran is best avoided immediately before which investigation?
explanation: Dextran forms rouleaux and interferes with cross-matching.
Take the cross-match sample before giving dextran.

mcqs.stem: Which route of fluid replacement is preferred when the gut is working and the deficit is modest?
explanation: Use the gut when it works and the deficit is modest.
Oral replacement is appropriate; IV is for a non-functioning gut or rapid needs.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Choose the least invasive effective route.

mcqs.stem: A serum potassium rise to about 5 mmol/L triggers which protective response?

options.text: Aldosterone secretion enhancing renal K excretion

explanation: Rising potassium stimulates aldosterone.
Aldosterone increases renal potassium excretion.
keyFacts: K rise → aldosterone → renal K loss.

mcqs.stem: Muscle weakness, paralytic ileus and slurred speech in a post-operative patient on prolonged nasogastric aspiration suggest:

options.why: Presents with different features and ECG.
Not the typical surgical cause here.

explanation: Prolonged aspiration depletes potassium.
Weakness, ileus and slurred speech are hypokalaemic features.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Link the losses to the deficit.

mcqs.stem: In sodium excess, the serum sodium concentration is typically:
explanation: Total-body sodium excess expands water proportionally.
So serum sodium is usually normal; oedema is the sign.
keyFacts: Sodium excess → normal serum Na, oedema.

mcqs.stem: A standard maintenance bag is typically supplemented with how much potassium chloride per litre?
explanation: Maintenance bags usually carry 20 mmol KCl.
The safe ceiling is 40 mmol per litre.

mcqs.stem: Which is a dilutional (hypervolaemic) cause of hyponatraemia?
explanation: Dilutional causes expand water relative to sodium.
Heart failure (and cirrhosis, ADH excess, salt-free fluid) is dilutional.

mcqs.stem: Which colloid has the longest quoted half-life and does not interfere with cross-matching?
explanation: Hetastarch has a 16–24 h half-life.
It does not interfere with cross-matching but is expensive and dose-limited.
keyFacts: Hetastarch: long half-life, no cross-match issue.

mcqs.stem: Above roughly which serum potassium does intracardiac conduction slow with risk of arrest?

options.why: This level triggers aldosterone but is not the arrest threshold.
Concerning but the quoted threshold for conduction slowing is ~7.

explanation: Rising potassium first tents T waves.
Above ~7 mmol/L conduction slows with arrhythmia and arrest risk.

mcqs.stem: The potassium deficit in an adult is estimated by which formula?
explanation: Deficit uses the gap from ~4.5 mmol/L.
Deficit ≈ (4.5 − serum K) × 100.

mcqs.stem: Hartmann's solution is best avoided as the sole fluid in a patient with:

options.why: Hartmann's is near-isotonic; not the key concern.

explanation: Hartmann's contains ~5 mmol/L potassium.
In established hyperkalaemia/renal failure this adds to the load.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Match the fluid to the electrolyte state.

mcqs.stem: Rapid over-correction of chronic hyponatraemia specifically risks:

options.why: That is a risk of hyponatraemia itself, not of correction.

explanation: Chronic hyponatraemia adapts the brain osmotically.
Rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis).

mcqs.stem: Which drug most typically produces hypokalaemia?

options.why: Correct — a loop diuretic causing potassium loss.
An ACE inhibitor tends to raise potassium.

explanation: Loop diuretics increase renal potassium loss.
Furosemide is the classic culprit.

mcqs.stem: Which change makes cells MORE excitable and can precipitate cardiac arrest?

options.why: Shifts potassium, not the direct answer.

explanation: Hyperkalaemia lowers the membrane excitation potential.
Cells become more excitable; above ~7 mmol/L arrest may follow.

mcqs.stem: Which crystalloid contains bicarbonate and calcium?
explanation: Balanced fluids add physiological ions.
Hartmann's includes bicarbonate and calcium.

mcqs.stem: 5% dextrose is used clinically to:

options.why: It distributes as water, not a durable expander.
It is combined with insulin for that.
Crystalloid saline/blood is used, not free water.

explanation: Metabolism of dextrose leaves water.
5% dextrose therefore replaces water.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Use dextrose for water, not volume.

mcqs.stem: A cirrhotic patient with ascites has serum Na⁺ 128 mmol/L and is clinically fluid-overloaded. Initial management is:

options.why: This adds sodium/water to an overloaded patient.
Not the first specific step for the sodium.

explanation: Cirrhosis causes dilutional (hypervolaemic) hyponatraemia.
Initial management is water restriction.

mcqs.stem: Which endocrine disorder causes sodium and water retention with hypertension and oedema?

options.why: Causes catecholamine-driven hypertension, not this pattern.

explanation: Aldosterone retains sodium and water.
Conn's syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism.

mcqs.stem: Which maintenance regimen delivers the higher daily sodium load?
explanation: Regimen A includes a litre of normal saline.
It delivers ~150 mmol Na versus ~90 mmol in regimen B.
keyFacts: Regimen A > regimen B for sodium.

mcqs.stem: A U wave with ST depression and a flat T wave on ECG indicates:

options.why: Gives peaked T and wide QRS.

explanation: A U wave with ST depression and flat T is hypokalaemic.
Contrast with the peaked T of hyperkalaemia.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Read the potassium off the ECG.

mcqs.stem: Which is NOT one of the three components considered when prescribing fluids?

options.why: Correct — not part of fluid prescription components.

options.text: Insensible losses added to the total

explanation: Prescribing considers basal needs, ongoing losses and pre-existing deficit.
Blood group is irrelevant to the maintenance calculation.

mcqs.stem: Which colloid is expensive, natural, and carries a small anaphylaxis risk?
explanation: Albumin is a natural blood-derived colloid.
It is expensive with a small anaphylaxis risk.
keyFacts: Albumin: natural, costly, small anaphylaxis risk.

mcqs.stem: After giving calcium gluconate for hyperkalaemia, the next priority is to:

options.text: Stop all treatment as the heart is protected
options.why: Serum K is still high and must be lowered.

options.text: Shift potassium into cells with insulin-dextrose
Give another dose of calcium only

explanation: Calcium protects but does not lower potassium.
Follow with insulin-dextrose (± bicarbonate) to shift K, then remove it.

emqs.instruction: For each scenario, select the single most likely electrolyte abnormality.

stems.stem: A patient on renal replacement misses dialysis; ECG shows peaked T waves and a widening QRS.
stems.why: Peaked T waves and wide QRS with missed dialysis indicate hyperkalaemia.

stems.stem: Prolonged nasogastric aspiration with weakness, ileus and a U wave on ECG.
stems.why: GI losses and a U wave indicate hypokalaemia.

stems.stem: Confusion after large volumes of 5% dextrose post-operatively; Na⁺ 119 mmol/L, no volume depletion.
stems.why: Salt-free fluid with a low sodium and normal volume is dilutional hyponatraemia.

stems.stem: Severe diarrhoea with sunken eyes, low CVP and Na⁺ 129 mmol/L.
stems.why: Low-volume signs with low sodium indicate depletional hyponatraemia.

emqs.instruction: Select the single best-matching agent for each intended action.

stems.stem: Immediate myocardial membrane stabilisation without lowering serum K.
stems.why: Calcium antagonises potassium at the membrane.

stems.stem: Drives potassium into cells while glucose prevents hypoglycaemia.
stems.why: Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium intracellularly.

stems.stem: Removes potassium from the body via the gastrointestinal tract.
stems.why: Ion-exchange resin binds and removes potassium enterally.

stems.stem: Definitive removal when all pharmacological measures fail.
stems.why: Dialysis is definitive for refractory hyperkalaemia.

emqs.instruction: For each requirement, select the single most appropriate fluid.

stems.stem: Restoring extracellular volume in a hypovolaemic, depleted patient.
Providing free water to a patient needing water replacement.
stems.why: 5% dextrose delivers free water after metabolism.

stems.stem: A balanced resuscitation fluid closest to plasma electrolytes.
stems.why: Hartmann's is the balanced, near-plasma option.

stems.stem: Cautious correction of severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.
stems.why: 3% (hypertonic) saline is used for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.

emqs.instruction: For each statement about IV potassium, select the correct value or rule.

stems.stem: The safe ceiling for concentration in a bag.
stems.why: No more than 40 mmol should be added per litre.

stems.stem: The safe ceiling for infusion rate.
stems.why: Potassium is given no faster than 40 mmol/hour.
Potassium must never be given as a bolus.

summary: Hyponatraemia (<135 mmol/L) is dilutional (salt-free fluid, ADH excess, CHF/cirrhosis → water restriction, cautious 3% saline if severe) or depletional (GI/renal/ECF losses → saline/Hartmann's); correct slowly to avoid central pontine myelinolysis. Sodium excess shows oedema with a usually-normal serum sodium. Hypokalaemia (vomiting, aspiration, diuretics, alkalosis) gives a U wave and needs cautious infused potassium, never a bolus. Hyperkalaemia (renal failure, acidosis) tents T waves and is managed by calcium (protect), insulin-dextrose/bicarbonate (shift), then resin/dialysis (remove). Daily needs are ~35 mL/kg water and ~1 mmol/kg each of Na and K; know normal saline (Na 154), Hartmann's (balanced) and the standard maintenance regimens, adding for fever and losses.
